$comment: Structural spine. These are the grouping nodes that hold the per-subsystem fragments together, plus the three navigation entries that guarantee the deep trunks (metals, petrochemicals, industry) and the bundled/required-peripheral branches are reachable from the root even if no fragment references them by id. Three of the five are deliberately kind `note`: they are indexes, not things in the supply chain, and they keep their children because data/00-root.json references them by id and this pass does not own that file.

roots.name: Mainboard ASSY 250407
roots.description: A single two-layer FR-4 board carrying the whole computer: 1.6 mm of laminate with 35 um of copper on each face, about 1200 unplated component holes, and not one plated-through hole or via anywhere on it. Eight 4164 64 Kbit DRAMs give the 64 KB of main RAM and one 2114L static chip holds 1 KB of screen colour; a 6510 at about 1 MHz, the 6567 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, two 6526 CIAs, a 6532 PPI, a mask-programmed 906114-01 PLA and three mask ROMs - 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL and the 4 KB 901225-01 character generator - do the rest. Everything is through-hole DIP, so every connection between two parts is a copper trace: where a later revision has a via, this board carries a short single-core jumper wire soldered across the same pads. About 320 components in all: 19 memory, custom-logic and ROM devices, about a dozen 74-series glue parts, a few CMOS parts and a handful of small-signal transistors.

facts.label: Board
facts.value: ASSY 250407, PCB 326498-01, material no. 250406, artwork 251137, schematic 251138

facts.label: Jumper wires
facts.value: 2 (E1, E2) across pads where a later revision has a via

facts.label: Mask ROM
facts.value: 20 KB total: 8 KB BASIC + 8 KB KERNAL + 4 KB character generator

roots.note: The 250407 is the long 'breadbin' layout and the U-numbers quoted throughout this tree are its canonical set; they do not line up with the 250425, 250466 or short boards. The via count is the one a validated copy of the 250407 artwork settles: zero, which is why the zero-via claim is stated in the description rather than left as a footnote. This node no longer lists c64.connector-jacks or c64.mains among its children: the plugs belong to the panel they are soldered into, which c64.io-panel carries, and the line cord, plug, switch and fuse live in the external power supply, which is a separate assembly reached from the top of the tree.

roots.name: Connectors and operator controls
roots.description: Everything that plugs into the machine, and the three things a person touches to run it. The rear edge of the board carries the 44-pin cartridge expansion socket, the integral RF modulator with its channel adjust and RCA antenna socket, an 8-pin DIN for composite video plus separate luma and chroma and audio in and out, the 6-pin DIN serial bus, the 2 x 6 card-edge datasette port and the 24-pin card-edge user port, and the panel also takes a 7-pin DIN power input and two DE-9 control ports. Power arrives as 5 V DC and 9 V AC on that 7-pin socket rather than as mains, because the transformer, rectifier and regulators are in the external supply - which is why the machine's own earthing arrangement is an interwinding screen and a bond inside the brick. The operator controls are a power rocker in the right-hand case panel and two slide potentiometers on the top deck, one for volume and tone and one for brightness, wired straight into the SID's audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.

facts.label: Video / audio
facts.value: 8-pin round DIN, 262-degree horseshoe: composite out, separate Y and C out, audio in and out

facts.label: Serial bus
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN, Commodore's serial variant of the IEEE-488 handshake, 300 baud

facts.label: Datasette
facts.value: 2 x 6 card edge: read, write, sense, motor, +5 V and ground

facts.label: User port
facts.value: 24-pin card edge: 17 TTL signals plus 7 ground and voltage pins, one of them 9 V AC

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: 44-pin dual-row card edge carrying the CPU address and data buses

facts.label: Power input
facts.value: 7-pin round DIN: 5 V DC and 9 V AC from the external supply

facts.label: RF modulator
facts.value: integral on the breadbin; RCA antenna output, channel set on the board by a trimmer

roots.note: Checked against c64.connector-jacks, which carries one subtree per connector - user port, cassette port, expansion port, video/audio DIN, serial DIN, control ports and power inlet - plus the shared contact-stamping and housing-moulding sequences and one connector deliberately left off this list, the keyboard ribbon header, which is an internal board-to-board header rather than something a user plugs into. Two qualifications worth keeping: the earliest boards, PCB 326498, carry a 5-pin DIN video connector with composite and luminance but no chroma, the 8-pin part appearing part-way through production; and this subtree is listed once, here, rather than also hanging off the mainboard.

roots.name: Where every branch terminates
roots.description: Everything above ends in one of three trunks: refined metals, petrochemicals, and the plants and utilities that supply both. Most component subtrees carry their own shorter copy of the relevant chain - a capacitor really does carry its own aluminium, and an ABS case really does carry its own acrylonitrile - so these are the canonical, deepest versions of the same chains, kept together so that one can be read end to end.
roots.note: An index of where the supply chains bottom out, not a plant: nothing is made, mined or operated here. It is the only route from the root to the metal, chemical and industrial branches, and the unlinked catalogue is parked here, so any canonical subtree that no branch links stays reachable rather than being dropped. Not established: that every branch terminates in one of three trunks - several subtrees bottom out at process equipment or at plant utilities rather than at a refined metal or a petrochemical, so the three-trunk claim is a simplification of the tree's own shape and is not a documented supply-chain fact.

roots.name: Finishing and bundled extras
roots.description: Three branches that hang off the machine rather than being part of it: how legends and colours were printed onto moulded plastic, how one keyboard key becomes a bit in the matrix, and the joystick that shipped in the box in some markets. None of them is needed to trace the machine's own supply line - they are the finishing and the bundled accessories, gathered here so they are not mistaken for part of the board.
roots.note: A grouping rather than a plant. Its three children are real things: decoration is a set of processes, the keyboard switches are parts, the joystick is a part. Two of the three are not interconnect goods, so the branch sits with the machine rather than with the interconnects it happens to be stored beside. Not established: which joystick shipped in the box in which market - Commodore's own documentation does not state a standard bundled joystick, so the three-child grouping is a convenience rather than a documented shipping configuration.
